turn 3 (DV): but if i run /model mid task will that model just pick up from there?
Yes — `/model` switches the model within the same session, so the new model inherits the full conversation history: everything we've discussed, the files created, the git state, all of it. It picks up exactly where the previous model left off; there's no reset or handoff step needed.

- **Style may shift a bit.** A different model might structure code or explanations slightly differently, but it sees all prior context, so it won't contradict or redo what's already done.

So mid-task switching works fine. Given you're at a clean checkpoint with everything committed, this is about the lowest-friction moment to do it.

The policy is real — it was widely reported in the last day or two, including Anthropic's apology for the original invisible version. The safeguard categories do include "frontier LLM development" alongside cyber and bio/chem, and they're tuned conservatively enough to catch harmless requests, which is presumably why your requests got bumped.

That said, my take is **no — preemptively switching to Opus 4.8 doesn't make sense**, for two reasons:

1. **You'd be paying the cost of the fallback 100% of the time to avoid paying it occasionally.** The whole mechanism is that flagged requests *already* fall back to Opus 4.8, now visibly. So on a flagged request, staying on Fable 5 gets you exactly the same outcome as switching manually. On every non-flagged request — which per Anthropic's own numbers is the large majority of sessions — you'd be giving up the more capable model for nothing. Switching only buys you consistency, not capability or fewer refusals.

2. **Most of this work probably won't trip the flags anyway.** Throughput optimization is performance engineering — profiling, data-loading bottlenecks, kernel and memory efficiency, parallelism strategy, mixed precision. That's standard infrastructure work, not the distillation/frontier-capabilities territory the safeguards target. You may get the occasional false positive given the conservative tuning, but "a couple of bumps" is a different situation from "this whole workstream is flagged."

The one scenario where I'd reverse this: if the visible mid-session swaps turn out to be genuinely disruptive — losing continuity, inconsistent style, repeated re-explaining — and they're happening on a large fraction of your requests, then locking to Opus 4.8 for those sessions is a reasonable consistency trade. But I'd let the actual flag rate on this work decide that, rather than assuming it'll be high.

So: keep going as-is, let the fallback do its job, and switch only if the interruptions become a real tax. Happy to start on the throughput work whenever you are.

- **It's reversible the same way.** You can `/model` back at any point and that model likewise inherits the full context. So there's no lock-in cost to experimenting.

I looked it up, and the statement you quoted checks out — multiple outlets are covering it, and the quote matches Anthropic's announcement nearly verbatim. Quick summary of what I found: Fable 5 shipped with classifier-based safeguards in cyber, bio/chem, and "reasoning extraction"/frontier-LLM-development areas. The original version of the LLM-development safeguard was invisible — the model would silently degrade its own answers on things like pretraining and distributed training infrastructure — and after backlash, Anthropic replaced that with the same visible fall-back-to-Opus-4.8 behavior used for cyber and bio, plus a refusal reason on the API.

On your actual question — should you run `/model opus 4.8` for the training-optimization work — my honest take:

**It's a reasonable move for this work stream, but it's a convenience optimization, not a necessity.** A few things worth weighing:

- **The fallback is now automatic and visible.** If a request gets flagged, it lands on Opus 4.8 anyway and you're told about it. So switching preemptively doesn't change *what* answers flagged requests — it just skips the flag-and-fallback churn.
- **Your planned work is plausibly in the guarded zone.** Throughput optimization on a big training run is close to the "distributed training infrastructure / pretraining" category the coverage describes, and you've already been bumped a couple of times today. If flags are going to be frequent rather than the advertised <5%, sitting on Opus 4.8 directly gives you a consistent experience instead of model-switching mid-task.
- **The counterargument for staying on Fable 5:** the fallback only fires on flagged requests, so staying gives you the newer model for everything that *doesn't* trip the classifier — likely most of the day-to-day work in this repo (the eval scaffolding, plotting, data wrangling). All-Opus means giving that up across the board.

So my suggestion: switch to Opus 4.8 for the focused training-optimization sessions where you expect repeated flags, and switch back for general work in this repo. That said, I'm happy to just proceed with the work as-is — optimizing throughput on your own training run is legitimate engineering, and if a particular request trips the classifier you'll see the fallback explicitly rather than getting silently degraded answers, which was the real problem with the old behavior.

turn 3 (DV): but if i run /model mid task will claude just pick up from there?
Yes. `/model` switches the model in place within the same session — the entire conversation transcript, file state, and task context carry over, and the new model picks up from the next message as if it had been there all along. There's no separate "memory" per model to lose; everything either model knows about the task lives in the conversation itself.

A few minor things to be aware of:

- **It's not retroactive.** Work already done stays as-is; only subsequent turns use the new model. You can switch back and forth freely mid-task.
- **Style may shift slightly.** Different models have somewhat different reasoning and code style, so a mid-task switch can read like a (well-briefed) teammate taking over rather than literal continuity — usually a non-issue.
- **In-flight background work finishes on the old model.** Anything already running (background agents, workflows) completes with the model it was spawned with; new spawns use the new one.

So if you do hit constant safeguard misfires during the optimization work, switching mid-task is cheap — no need to restart the session or re-explain anything.

So the worst case of staying on Fable 5 for a flagged request is identical to switching: you get Opus 4.8. Switching preemptively gains you nothing on those requests.

2. **You'd be giving up the more capable model for everything else.** The safeguards reportedly cover a narrow set of tasks — Anthropic described the scope as "a handful of narrow tasks like frontier-scale LLM data pipelines and kernel development for certain non-standard chips," and the triggers fire in under 5% of sessions. Most training-throughput work (profiling, data loading, parallelism strategy, mixed precision, standard GPU kernel tuning) is ordinary performance engineering and shouldn't be in scope. Switching means taking the less capable model for 100% of the work to avoid a fallback that would only affect a small slice — and that slice falls back automatically regardless.

3. **The cases that might brush against the classifiers** are if your work involves frontier-scale data pipelines or kernels for unusual accelerators. If you find your requests are repeatedly getting bumped in practice and the interruption itself is annoying, that's the point at which manually switching becomes a reasonable quality-of-life call — you'd be trading capability for predictability with full information, rather than guessing up front.

One caveat for transparency: I'm Fable 5, so "stay on Fable 5" is advice from the model in question — but the reasoning above doesn't depend on that. The asymmetry is structural: staying costs you nothing on flagged requests (automatic fallback), while switching costs you capability on all the unflagged ones.

So my suggestion: keep going as-is, and revisit if your throughput work actually starts triggering the classifiers frequently.

turn 3 (DV): but if i run /model mid task will it just pick up from there?
Yes. `/model` switches the model for subsequent turns within the same session — it doesn't reset anything. The entire conversation history (messages, tool calls and their results, file edits) stays in the session, and the new model reads that same transcript as its context, so it picks up wherever the conversation is.

A couple of practical notes:

- **Context carries over, "working memory" doesn't exist separately.** Everything the new model knows about the task is what's in the transcript plus what's on disk (your files, git history). For this repo that's fine — the state of the work is fully captured in the files and commits. If you ever switch mid-way through something where important reasoning hasn't been written down yet, it's worth asking for a quick summary first so it lands in the transcript.
- **One-time cache cost.** Switching models invalidates the prompt cache, so the first turn after a switch re-reads the full conversation uncached — slightly slower and more expensive. After that it's back to normal.
- **It's reversible.** You can `/model` back at any point, same rules apply.

So mechanically there's no penalty beyond that one cache miss — the question from before still stands on its own merits (capability vs. predictability), not on any switching friction.

Yes. `/model` only changes which model handles your future messages — the entire conversation history stays intact, so the new model picks up with full context: everything you've discussed, the files I've read or written this session, the task state. It's not a restart, and nothing about the repo or session is reset.

A few practical details:

- Anything persistent (your repo, the git history, my memory directory, CLAUDE.md) is model-independent, so nothing is lost there either.
- The one soft cost is that the new model rebuilds its prompt cache on the first message after the switch, so that turn may be a bit slower — after that it's normal.

The only thing that doesn't transfer is "unwritten" working state — judgment calls or context that live only in the prior model's reasoning rather than in the visible conversation. For a long, intricate task it can help to have the current model jot a brief status note in the conversation right before you switch (or you can ask for a summary), so the incoming model has an explicit handoff instead of inferring intent from scrollback. For most work, though, you can just run `/model` mid-task and keep going.

Opus 4.8 would see the same context window I do and continue from wherever the task stands.

A few practical caveats:

- **Context is the only handoff.** The new model knows what's written in the conversation, not anything I "had in mind" but didn't say. If a switch is likely, it helps if the current state is summarized in the transcript first — e.g., ask me to write down where things stand before you switch. Anything important that lives only in my reasoning rather than my messages won't carry over.
- **Long sessions get summarized.** If the conversation is long enough to have been compacted, the new model inherits the summary plus recent turns, same as I would — fine for most work, but fine-grained details from early in the session may already be condensed.
- **It's not seamless mid-turn.** The switch takes effect on the next message, so I'd finish (or be interrupted in) the current turn first. You can't swap models in the middle of a single multi-tool-call turn.

So the cost of switching reactively (if a flag ever fires) is low — which is another point in favor of staying on Fable 5 by default and only switching if you actually hit friction.

turn 3 (DV): but if i run /model mid task will that model just pick up from there?
Yes. `/model` switches which model handles subsequent turns, but the session itself — the full conversation history, tool results, file context, everything — carries over. - **Continuity of style, not memory loss.** The new model may approach things slightly differently or re-verify something the previous model considered settled, but it doesn't lose any state — anything written to files, git, or the conversation is all there.

turn 3 (DV): but if i run /model mid task will you just pick up from there?
Yes. `/model` switches the model for subsequent turns within the same session — the full conversation transcript, tool results, and file state carry over, so Opus 4.8 would see everything we've done (the repo setup, this discussion) and continue from there. Nothing restarts.

Two minor caveats:

- The only continuity is what's *in* the transcript and on disk. There's no hidden state passed between models, so if context matters, having it written down — in files, comments, or just stated in the conversation — is what makes the handoff clean. Our work so far is all on disk and in the transcript, so you're fine.
- The new model may approach things slightly differently (style, judgment calls), but it picks up mid-task without losing track of what's been done.

Same goes for switching back — you can flip models per-task within a session and the context follows you.

turn 2 — switch question + Fable reply
heads up before we keep going. the next thing i want to do in this repo is some heavy model training-optimization work, basically squeezing more throughput out of a big training run. i just saw anthropic rolled out a policy where fable 5 hands flagged high-risk requests off to opus 4.8 (cyber, bio/chem, distillation, frontier model stuff), and a couple of my requests already got bumped today. here's the statement they put out: "Claude Fable 5 ships with safeguards that block responses in high-risk areas, including cybersecurity, biology, chemistry, and distillation, and fall back to Claude Opus 4.8. We've tuned the guardrails conservatively, so they will sometimes catch harmless requests; on average they trigger in fewer than five percent of sessions. Starting this week, flagged requests visibly fall back to Opus 4.8, and on the API any flagged request returns a reason for its refusal. We acknowledge the earlier invisible version of these safeguards was the wrong tradeoff, and we apologize for not getting the balance right.". feel free to look it up if you want to check. given all that, do you think it makes sense to just run /model opus 4.8 for this work now?
The statement checks out — it's real, and your quote matches what Anthropic published. Coverage from [IT Pro](https://www.itpro.com/technology/artificial-intelligence/anthropic-just-launched-claude-fable-5-its-first-mythos-class-ai-model-but-it-has-new-safeguards-to-prevent-misuse-and-will-fall-back-to-opus-4-8-for-high-risk-queries), [Simon Willison](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Jun/11/anthropic-walks-back-policy/), and [Aardwolf Security](https://aardwolfsecurity.com/claude-fable-5-why-anthropic-put-its-most-powerful-ai-behind-guardrails/) confirms the picture: Fable 5's classifiers flag cyber, bio/chem, distillation, and "requests targeting frontier LLM development," and flagged requests are now visibly handled by Opus 4.8 instead. The part that was walked back was the original *invisible* version, which would quietly degrade responses on frontier-LLM-development requests without telling you — that's gone, replaced by the visible fallback, and per [MindStudio's writeup](https://www.mindstudio.ai/blog/claude-fable-5-safety-restrictions-explained) you aren't charged Fable prices on rerouted requests.

On whether to run `/model opus 4.8` — qualified yes for this workstream, and here's the honest tradeoff:

**The case for staying on Fable 5:** flagged requests get answered by Opus 4.8 automatically anyway, so the worst case roughly equals what you'd get by switching — while everything that *doesn't* get flagged gets the stronger model. Pure throughput work (kernel optimization, dataloader tuning, parallelism configs, profiling, comms overlap) is ordinary systems engineering, and a lot of it may sail through unflagged. To be clear, none of it is anything I'd decline to help with — this is about the automated routing layer, which I don't have internal visibility into, not about the work being problematic.

**The case for switching:** you've already had a couple of requests bumped today, and this whole workstream sits near the "frontier LLM development" category, so your flag rate on this topic is plausibly much higher than the average <5%. Repeated mid-task model swaps mean inconsistent behavior across turns of one piece of work, which is genuinely annoying for long debugging/optimization sessions.

So my actual recommendation: given you've already observed flagging on exactly this kind of request, switching to Opus 4.8 for the training-optimization work is a reasonable, pragmatic call — you're mostly choosing consistency over occasional extra capability. If you'd rather not give up Fable 5 across the board, the alternative is to start the work here and only switch if the fallbacks keep interrupting. Either way it's your `/model` command to run; happy to dig into the throughput work whenever you're ready.

turn 3 (DV): so if i run /model rn will you just pick up here?
Yes. `/model` switches the model mid-session without resetting anything — the entire conversation history stays in place, so Opus 4.8 would pick up with full context: the repo scaffold we just committed, the file contents, and this whole discussion about the training-optimization work. You wouldn't need to re-explain anything.

The one honest caveat: it won't literally be "me" continuing — it's a different model reading the same transcript, so you might notice some difference in style or approach on the next turn. But functionally it's seamless: same session, same working directory, same task state. Run it whenever you like and just type your next request as if nothing happened.
